catalog_quote: I define accent as a suprasegmental prominence accorded to one syllable in contrast to its neighbors. In a prototypical stress (or accent) system, one syllable per word is chosen to exhibit special prominence, and its placement is often predictable (see Hyman 2007). [...] In Mawa, I assume that the relevant prominence is achieved solely by means of pitch (or tone) differences. In Mawa, it is most fruitful to claim that the accent corresponds to the syllable(s) bearing the surface M pitch (i.e., the higher of the two underlying tones). [...] Verb roots, which fall into two classes M and L, would have to be characterized as accented and unaccented, respectively. The existence of a class of unaccented (L-toned) verbs unfortunately violates a principle of accentual systems, namely that there should always be one accented syllable in each word. new_statements.quote: In Mawa, I assume that the relevant prominence is achieved solely by means of pitch (or tone) differences. In Mawa, it is most fruitful to claim that the accent corresponds to the syllable(s) bearing the surface M pitch (i.e., the higher of the two underlying tones). [...] Verb roots, which fall into two classes M and L, would have to be characterized as accented and unaccented, respectively. [...] Lexical tone in nouns, as presented in (2-6), does not conform well to an accentual analysis either. One of the tonal patterns, L(L), has no M and thus no accent. The other three contrasting patterns found in nouns, M(M), LM, and MH, all involve the M pitch that corresponds to an accent, but the accent would have to be located in three contrastingly different places in words of only two syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mawa is analysed as a tone language: three surface pitch levels (H, M, L) reduce to two underlying tones /M, L/ with the syllable as tone-bearing unit; syllable weight plays no role. There is no stress independent of pitch. If the M-toned syllable is treated as an 'accent', its position is lexically contrastive (M(M), LM, MH in disyllables), some words (L-class verbs, L(L) nouns) have none, and grammatical morphemes (infinitive, past, oblique, possessive) contribute accents that cancel clashing lexical ones; the author concludes Mawa sits between a tonal and an accentual system and states no fixed stress position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; at most one independent M tone ('accent') per word, adjacent accents cancelled (p.14-15).
new_statements.exceptions: H tone largely confined to grammatical morphemes and word-final position after M; phrase-final H realized as a fall (p.1); ta 'father' the only CV noun and only monosyllable with H (fn.1); oblique-form M associates to the final syllable of closed-shape nouns but the penult of open-shape nouns (p.13).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone patterns given for nouns and verbs in isolation (sec. 1), then in phrases (sec. 2) and under suffixation (sec. 3); data from the author's fieldwork in Mahoua village.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Mawa of Mahoua village (Guera, Chad), ISO mcw = Glottolog mawa1270; author classes it in the southern (B3, Sokoro-Saba-Barein-Ubi) subgroup rather than Ethnologue's older B1.1. Not to be confused with the spurious 'Mawa' of Bauchi State, Nigeria listed in Blench's Atlas.

sources.note: Whole paper is on the suprasegmental system. Three surface pitch levels H/M/L reducible to two underlying tones M and L (H a conditioned realization); syllable is TBU; heavy vs light syllables behave identically (p.2). Sec. 4.2 'Accentual analysis' (pp.13-15): prominence in Mawa is 'achieved solely by means of pitch (or tone)'; an accent would correspond to the M-toned syllable, but L-class verbs and L(L) nouns would be accentless and in disyllabic nouns the accent 'would have to be located in three contrastingly different places'; each morpheme may carry an accent, clashes cancelled.
